about.title: Chowchilla Product Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Defective products cause harm everywhere, and Chowchilla is no exception — whether it's a piece of farm equipment along Robertson Boulevard, a faulty vehicle part on SR-99, or a household appliance that malfunctions at home. California law gives injured people an important advantage: strict liability. That means you generally don't have to prove a manufacturer was careless, only that the product itself was defective in design, manufacturing, or warning, and that the defect caused your injury. Liability can extend beyond the maker to distributors and retailers who sold the item. If you've been hurt by something that didn't work the way it should have, LawProactive can connect you with an independent attorney familiar with these claims, free of charge. The first step is often the simplest: hold onto the product, don't repair or discard it, and get guidance on what comes next.

items.title: Strict Liability Works in Your Favor
items.desc: California doesn't require you to prove the manufacturer was negligent, just that the product was defective and caused your injury. That's a meaningful difference for someone recovering from a serious injury.

items.title: Multiple Parties May Share Responsibility
items.desc: Manufacturers, distributors, and retailers can all be pursued for a defective product, which broadens the paths available to seek compensation.

items.title: Preserving Evidence Matters Early On
items.desc: Keeping the defective product intact, rather than repairing or discarding it, can be critical to building a claim, and an attorney can guide you through that from the start.

items.question: What counts as a defective product under California law?
items.answer: A product can be defective in three ways: a design flaw that makes it unsafe even when made correctly, a manufacturing error that caused a specific unit to be faulty, or a failure to warn users of a known risk. California's strict liability standard means you focus on the product's condition and the harm it caused, not on proving carelessness.

items.question: I was hurt by farm equipment near Chowchilla — does that count as product liability?
items.answer: It can, depending on what caused the injury. If a mechanical failure or design flaw in the equipment led to your injury, rather than simple wear or misuse, that may fall under product liability rather than a workplace claim. An independent attorney can review the details and help sort out which type of claim applies.

items.question: Do I need to keep the product that hurt me?
items.answer: Yes, if at all possible. The product itself is often the most important piece of evidence in a defect claim, so avoid repairing, modifying, or throwing it away until you've spoken with an attorney.
